inputs.need:
I coordinate the school immunization program for the Brenmoor District Health Department, which covers 41 secondary schools and about 23,000 students in grades 7 to 9. After two disrupted school years, many students missed the adolescent vaccines we give in school: HPV, meningococcal ACWY and the tetanus, diphtheria and pertussis booster. From March to May 2026 we ran a catch-up campaign. Nurses visited every school twice, consent forms went home on paper and by text message, and each of our four towns had a Saturday clinic.

We now need to know what coverage we achieved, and for whom, so that next year's program goes where the gaps are. My problem is that I do not know which kind of study we can do. If the regional immunization register gives us student-level records with school and home postcode, we could follow the grade 7 to 9 students from before to after the campaign as a cohort and see who caught up. If the register only releases aggregate counts, we would need a cross-sectional coverage survey in a sample of schools, checking vaccination cards or asking parents. The register's data custodian has not answered the request we sent in June.

I also want to understand why consent forms did not come back from some schools, and whether the remaining gaps follow neighbourhood deprivation or the language spoken at home. We have one epidemiologist two days a week and the program nurses during school hours, and the school board has to approve anything that happens in schools.

The school board research committee meets quarterly; its next meeting is on 2026-11-18.

response.statement: A district catch-up campaign in spring 2026 offered the adolescent HPV, meningococcal ACWY and pertussis-containing vaccines to about 23,000 students in grades 7 to 9 across 41 schools after two disrupted school years. records.title: Catch-up of adolescent vaccines through school-located clinics after pandemic disruption: coverage by grade and school
records.authors: Haldane-Okoro M, Feng-Albright C, Duarte-Nkemelu S
records.abstract: We describe a school-located catch-up program in 58 secondary schools after two disrupted school years. Using register data from before and six months after the program, coverage of the adolescent HPV series rose from 54 to 71 percent, meningococcal ACWY from 68 to 83 percent and the pertussis-containing booster from 70 to 84 percent. Gains were smallest in schools in the most deprived quintile, where HPV coverage rose from 41 to 52 percent. Schools that sent consent reminders by text message had higher consent return. The analysis relied on a register whose completeness for adolescents was not assessed.

records.title: Completeness of a regional immunization register for adolescent vaccines compared with school vaccination cards
records.abstract: We compared register entries with vaccination cards for 1,480 students in 30 schools. The register agreed with the card for 91 percent of doses given in school programs and 78 percent of doses given in community clinics or pharmacies. Agreement was lowest for students who had moved into the region in the previous two years (64 percent). Register-based coverage underestimated card-based coverage by 4 to 9 percentage points, depending on the vaccine. The authors recommend a correction for doses given outside school programs when registers are used to measure coverage.

records.title: Paper forms and text message reminders for parental consent in school vaccination programs
records.authors: Mbeki-Lorenzo T, Whitfield-Arora N, Castell-Ibe O
records.abstract: In a program covering 44 schools, consent forms were sent home on paper, and from the second term parents also received text message reminders with a link to an electronic form. Consent return rose from 61 to 79 percent after reminders were added. The rise was smaller in schools where more than a third of families spoke a language other than the program language at home (from 52 to 63 percent), and electronic forms were used less by parents in those schools. Translated reminders were introduced late and could not be evaluated separately.

records.title: Neighbourhood deprivation and completion of adolescent vaccines in school programs: a cross-sectional analysis
records.abstract: Using linked school program and area data for 21,600 students, we examined HPV series completion by quintile of neighbourhood deprivation. Completion was 74 percent in the least deprived quintile and 49 percent in the most deprived, a gradient that persisted after adjustment for school and grade. Consent refusal explained less of the gap than consent forms that were never returned. Students absent on vaccination days were concentrated in the most deprived quintile. The analysis could not separate deprivation from the language spoken at home.

records.title: Cluster sampling for school vaccination coverage surveys: design effects from twelve surveys
records.abstract: We pooled data from twelve school-based vaccination coverage surveys that sampled schools and then students within schools. Design effects for coverage estimates ranged from 1.6 to 2.8, with a median of 2.1, and were largest where coverage differed most between schools. Checking vaccination cards changed estimates by up to 11 percentage points compared with parent report. Response was lower among students whose parents had to return a card or form. We provide design effects to plan sample sizes for future surveys.

records.title: Saturday community clinics as an adjunct to school vaccination: who attends?
records.venue: District public health service report series
records.abstract: Four district health units offered Saturday vaccination clinics alongside school visits during a catch-up campaign. Of 1,930 students vaccinated at Saturday clinics, 62 percent had missed a school visit through absence and 21 percent had returned a consent form too late for the school visit. Students from the most deprived neighbourhoods were under-represented at Saturday clinics relative to their share of missed doses. The report does not state its year of publication, and attendance was counted from clinic lists rather than the register.

response.synthesis: Six retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. A comparable catch-up program raised coverage by 14 to 17 points but least in deprived schools. The regional register captures school doses well and community doses less well, so a register-based follow-up is usable with a correction, while a cluster survey with a design effect near 2.1 is a workable fallback. Deprivation and unreturned consent forms explain much of the remaining gap, and text reminders helped least where families speak other languages. One undated report could not be judged for quality.

response.rationale: The right design depends on whether the register releases student-level records. With them, a register-based follow-up of all grade 7 to 9 students from before to after the campaign gives complete coverage by school and neighbourhood, corrected for doses given outside schools (c1). Without them, a two-stage cluster survey of schools with card checks gives an estimate with a design effect near 2.1 (c2). Choosing now would either waste the epidemiologist's time on a branch that cannot run or commit to a survey that the register might make unnecessary.
alternatives: Register-based follow-up of all grade 7 to 9 students (needs student-level access)
Two-stage cluster coverage survey with vaccination card checks (needs school board approval)
District totals from aggregate register counts (refused as the sole design: hides the school-level gaps)
response.whyNotMoreComplex: Running both branches in full would double the work for no gain; one decision from the custodian settles which branch runs.

decision.statement: Defer the choice between a register-based follow-up and a school cluster coverage survey until the register's data custodian decides on student-level access, and prepare both branches so that either can start in January 2027.

I coordinate the school immunization program for the Brenmoor District Health Department, which covers 41 secondary schools and about 23,000 students in grades 7 to 9. After two disrupted school years, many students missed the adolescent vaccines we give in school: HPV, meningococcal ACWY and the tetanus, diphtheria and pertussis booster. From March to May 2026 we ran a catch-up campaign. Nurses visited every school twice, consent forms went home on paper and by text message, and each of our four towns had a Saturday clinic.

We now need to know what coverage we achieved, and for whom, so that next year's program goes where the gaps are. My problem is that I do not know which kind of study we can do. If the regional immunization register gives us student-level records with school and home postcode, we could follow the grade 7 to 9 students from before to after the campaign as a cohort and see who caught up. If the register only releases aggregate counts, we would need a cross-sectional coverage survey in a sample of schools, checking vaccination cards or asking parents. The register's data custodian has not answered the request we sent in June.

I also want to understand why consent forms did not come back from some schools, and whether the remaining gaps follow neighbourhood deprivation or the language spoken at home. We have one epidemiologist two days a week and the program nurses during school hours, and the school board has to approve anything that happens in schools.
